title: Spanish grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday Spanish, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is everyday Mexican Spanish (with ustedes for “you all”, as all of Latin America says it).

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Spanish conversation.

goal.t: Hola, soy Ana. Soy de Chicago.
goal.tr: Hi, I'm Ana. I'm from Chicago.

dialog.tr: Hi! My name is Diego. What's your name?
Hi, Diego. I'm Ana.
Nice to meet you, Ana.
Likewise.
Where are you from?
I'm from Chicago. And you?
I'm from here, from Guadalajara.

blocks.p: **Saying who you are.** {{Soy}} means “I am”: {{Soy Ana.}} “I'm Ana.” With {{de}} “from”, it says where you're from: {{Soy de Chicago.}} You can also give your name with {{Me llamo…}}, word for word “I call myself…”: {{Me llamo Ana.}} Both are everyday Spanish.

blocks.means: a word for an action or a state: eat, go, live, be. {{Soy}} “I am” is a verb.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she, it.

blocks.p: **Spanish usually leaves out “I”.** The pronoun for “I” is {{yo}}, but {{soy}} already means “I am”, so Spanish normally leaves {{yo}} out: {{Soy de Chicago.}} Add {{yo}} only to stress it: {{Yo soy de Chicago, ¿y tú?}} “**I**'m from Chicago, and you?”

**Two words for “you”.** Spanish has a friendly “you”, {{tú}}, for friends, family, children and people your age in relaxed places, and a polite one, {{usted}}, for people you don't know, older people, and at work. The verb changes with them:
**Asking.** A question is written between ¿ and ?: the upside-down mark warns you a question is coming. The question word comes first: {{¿De dónde eres?}} is, word for word, “from where are you?”.

ex.tr: I'm Laura, nice to meet you.

ex.note: a question just by raising your voice at the end
polite: to someone you don't know

blocks.tip: Hello and goodbye: {{Hola}} (hi), {{Buenos días}} (good morning), {{Buenas tardes}} (good afternoon, from about noon), {{Buenas noches}} (good evening, good night), {{Adiós}} or {{Hasta luego}} (bye). The little mark on a vowel (á, é, í, ó, ú) shows the loudest part of the word ({{adiós}}: a-DIÓS) and sometimes tells two words apart: {{tú}} “you”, {{tu}} “your”.

mistakes.why: Without {{me}}, {{llamo}} means “I call”: {{Yo llamo Ana}} sounds like “I call Ana”. Your name is {{Me llamo…}}, “I call myself…”.
To an older man you don't know, use the polite {{usted}}, and the verb goes with it: {{es usted}}, not {{eres}}.

practice.q: You're meeting your new boss. How do you ask where she's from?
practice.why: At work, with someone you don't know well, use the polite {{usted}}: {{¿De dónde es usted?}}

practice.q: You're Mike, from Seattle. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: Hi! My name is Lucía. What's your name?

lines.why: About yourself: {{me llamo}}. {{Te llamas}} is “your name is”.

lines.tr: Nice to meet you, Mike. Where are you from?

lines.why: {{Soy}} for “I am”, and {{¿Y tú?}} turns the question back to her.

practice.q: Greet an older man politely and ask his name: “Good morning, what's your name?”
Your turn: say hello, your name and where you're from. Start with {{Hola, soy…}}

answers.t: Hola, soy Mike. Soy de Seattle.
answers.tr: Hi, I'm Mike. I'm from Seattle.

answers.t: Hola, me llamo Jennifer. Soy de Canadá.
answers.tr: Hi, my name is Jennifer. I'm from Canada.

lessons.title: Say who people are and what they do
lessons.summary: Introduce a friend and say what people do and where they're from: “She's a doctor. We're from Texas.”
lessons.topic: {{ser}} for everyone ({{soy, eres, es, somos, son}}); jobs without {{un}} or {{una}}; -o for men, -a for women

goal.t: Ella es Laura. Es doctora y es de Monterrey.
goal.tr: This is Laura. She's a doctor and she's from Monterrey.

dialog.t: Diego, ella es mi amiga Laura.
dialog.tr: Diego, this is my friend Laura.
Nice to meet you, Laura. Are you from here?
No, I'm from Monterrey.
And what do you do?
I'm a doctor. And you?

dialog.t: Soy maestro. Mi esposa y yo somos maestros.
dialog.tr: I'm a teacher. My wife and I are teachers.

blocks.p: **The verb {{ser}}.** {{Soy}} “I am” and {{eres}} “you are” are forms of one verb, {{ser}} “to be”. Here it is for everyone:

table: he is, she is, you are (polite)

blocks.p: {{Usted}} uses the same form as “he” and “she”: {{usted es}}. For more than one “you”, Mexico uses {{ustedes}} for everyone, friends and strangers alike: {{ustedes son}}. ({{Nosotras}} “we” and {{ellas}} “they” are for groups of women only.)

blocks.means: whether a word is masculine or feminine. In Spanish every word for a person or a thing has one, and the words around it change to match.

blocks.p: **Men and women.** Words for jobs and nationalities change with the person: usually **-o** for a man and **-a** for a woman: {{Él es mexicano. Ella es mexicana.}} A word ending in a consonant adds **-a** for a woman: {{doctor}} → {{doctora}}, {{profesor}} → {{profesora}}, {{inglés}} → {{inglesa}} (the accent mark goes). Words ending in **-e** or **-ista** stay the same: {{estudiante}}, {{dentista}}, {{estadounidense}} (American).

**No “a” before a job.** English says “She's **a** doctor”; Spanish says just {{Es doctora.}} The {{una}} comes back only when you describe the person: {{Es una doctora muy buena.}} “She's a very good doctor.”

ex.t: Ella es enfermera y él es mesero.
ex.tr: She's a nurse and he's a waiter.

ex.note: {{papás}}: dad and mom together. {{Mi}} “my”, {{mis}} for more than one (lesson 10).

blocks.tip: Nationalities and languages have no capital letter in Spanish: {{Soy estadounidense}}, {{Ella es mexicana}}, {{el español}}. Countries and cities do: {{México}}, {{Canadá}}.

mistakes.why: To say what someone does, just the job, without {{una}}.
Laura is a woman: {{mexicana}}, with -a.
“We are” is {{somos}}.

practice.tr: My wife and I are teachers.

practice.q: Your friend Carmen is a nurse. Which one is right?
practice.why: A woman: {{enfermera}}, with -a; and no {{una}} before a job.

practice.q: At a party, you introduce your friend Tom. Choose your replies.

options: Él es mi amigo Tom. Es de Boston.
Él soy mi amigo Tom. Soy de Boston.
lines.why: About him: {{es}}. {{Soy}} is only for “I am”.
Tom is a man: {{mesero}}; and just the job, without {{un}}.

practice.q: Your turn: introduce someone you know. Who are they, what do they do, where are they from? Start with {{Él es…}} or {{Ella es…}}

answers.t: Ella es mi hermana Kate. Es dentista y es de Ohio.
answers.tr: This is my sister Kate. She's a dentist and she's from Ohio.

answers.t: Él es mi amigo Ben. Es estudiante y es de California.
answers.tr: This is my friend Ben. He's a student and he's from California.

lessons.title: Say how you are and where you are
lessons.summary: Ask “How are you?” and answer, and say where you are right now: the other “to be”, {{estar}}.

goal.t: Estoy bien, gracias. Estoy en la oficina.
goal.tr: I'm fine, thanks. I'm at the office.

dialog.tr: Hi, son! How are you?

dialog.t: Bien, mamá, pero un poco cansado.
dialog.tr: Fine, Mom, but a little tired.
Where are you?

dialog.t: Estoy en el trabajo. ¿Y tú, cómo estás?
dialog.tr: I'm at work. And how are you?

dialog.t: Muy bien. Tu papá y yo estamos en casa.
dialog.tr: Very well. Your dad and I are at home.

blocks.p: **A second “to be”.** Spanish has two verbs for “to be”. You've met {{ser}}: who or what someone is ({{Soy Pablo}}, {{Soy maestro}}, {{Soy de Texas}}). The other one, {{estar}}, says **how** someone is right now and **where** someone or something is:

table: he is, she is, you are (polite)
you are (all of you), they are

blocks.p: Mind the accent marks: {{estás}}, {{está}}, {{están}} are said es-TÁS, es-TÁ, es-TÁN, loudest at the end.
**{{ser}} or {{estar}}?** A first rule that works most of the time: **{{ser}} for what someone or something is** (name, job, where they're from), **{{estar}} for how they are and where they are**.

table: {{Está en la escuela.}} She's at school.

ex.note: said by a woman; a man says {{contento}}

ex.t: El baño está a la derecha.
ex.tr: The bathroom is on the right.

blocks.p: Words for how you feel change for men and women, like jobs: {{cansado}} / {{cansada}} (tired), {{contento}} / {{contenta}} (happy), {{enfermo}} / {{enferma}} (sick), {{ocupado}} / {{ocupada}} (busy). {{Bien}} (well, fine) and {{mal}} (bad, not well) never change.

blocks.tip: {{¿Cómo estás?}} asks how you are; {{¿Cómo eres?}}, with {{ser}}, asks what you're like as a person. Answer {{¿Cómo estás?}} with {{Bien, gracias}}, {{Más o menos}} (so-so) or {{Muy bien, ¿y tú?}}

mistakes.why: Tired is how you are right now: {{estar}}.
Where someone is: {{estar}}.

practice.q: Which verb says where you are?
practice.why: Where someone or something is: {{estar}} ({{Estoy en casa}}).

practice.t: Mi hermana ___ en el hospital. Es enfermera.
practice.tr: My sister is at the hospital. She's a nurse.

practice.why: Where someone is from is part of who they are: {{ser}}, {{son}}.

practice.q: Your friend calls. Choose your replies.

lines.why: {{Bien}} on its own, or {{Estoy bien}}: never {{soy bien}}.
Where you are: {{estoy}}. ({{El súper}} is the supermarket.)

practice.q: Your turn: how are you today, and where are you right now? Answer with {{Estoy…}}

answers.t: Estoy bien, pero un poco cansado. Estoy en casa.
answers.tr: I'm fine, but a little tired. I'm at home.

answers.t: Estoy muy contenta. Estoy en el trabajo.
answers.tr: I'm very happy. I'm at work.

lessons.title: Name things: a, the and more than one
lessons.summary: Ask “What's this?” and name things, one or many: {{el libro}}, {{la mesa}}, {{unos tacos}}.
lessons.topic: nouns and their gender; {{el, la, los, las}} and {{un, una, unos, unas}}; plurals

dialog.tr: Excuse me, what's this?
It's a tamal with poblano peppers.
And that?

dialog.t: Es una gordita. Y aquí están los tamales de pollo.
dialog.tr: It's a gordita. And here are the chicken tamales.

dialog.t: Un tamal de pollo, por favor.
dialog.tr: A chicken tamal, please.

blocks.means: a word for a person, a place or a thing: friend, city, book, coffee.

blocks.p: **Every noun has a gender.** In Spanish not only people but things are masculine or feminine. There's no meaning to look for ({{libro}} “book” is masculine, {{mesa}} “table” is feminine), but the ending usually tells you: most nouns in **-o** are masculine, most in **-a** are feminine.

blocks.means: a little word before a noun: “the”, “a”.

blocks.p: **“The” and “a”** change with the gender, and with the number:

**More than one.** A noun ending in a vowel adds **-s**: {{taco}} → {{tacos}}. One ending in a consonant adds **-es**: {{ciudad}} → {{ciudades}} (city), {{flor}} → {{flores}} (flower). A final **-z** becomes **-ces**: {{lápiz}} → {{lápices}} (pencil).

**Learn each noun with its article.** A few break the -o/-a rule: {{el día}} (the day), {{el mapa}}, {{el problema}}, but {{la mano}} (the hand), {{la foto}}. Nouns ending in **-ción** and **-dad** are feminine: {{la canción}} (the song), {{la ciudad}}. Others you simply learn: {{el café}}, {{la calle}} (the street), {{el hotel}}, {{la noche}} (the night).

ex.note: in Mexico a pen is a {{pluma}}

ex.t: Las llaves están en la mesa.
ex.tr: The keys are on the table.

ex.t: El hotel está en el centro.
Un café y dos tamales, por favor.
ex.tr: A coffee and two tamales, please.

blocks.tip: {{esto}} “this” and {{eso}} “that” ask about something whose name you don't know: {{¿Qué es esto?}} They have no article and never change. The answer uses {{un}} or {{una}}: {{Es un tamal.}}

mistakes.why: {{problema}} ends in -a, but it's masculine, like {{el día}} and {{el mapa}}.
{{mesa}} is feminine: {{una}}.

practice.why: {{día}} ends in -a, but it's masculine: {{el día}}. Learn each noun with its article.
Nouns in -dad are feminine, and one ending in a consonant adds -es: {{las ciudades}}.

practice.q: At the market: choose your replies.

lines.tr: Come on in! What can I get you?

options: Un tamal y dos tacos, por favor.
Una tamal y dos tacos, por favor.

lines.t: Es un champurrado, una bebida de chocolate.
lines.tr: It's champurrado, a thick chocolate drink.

practice.q: Your turn: what's on your table right now? Name three things, with {{un}}, {{una}}, {{unos}} or {{unas}}.

answers.t: Un café, un celular y unas llaves.
answers.tr: A coffee, a cell phone and some keys.

answers.t: Una computadora, un libro y una pluma.
answers.tr: A computer, a book and a pen.

lessons.title: Describe people and things
lessons.summary: Say what people and things are like, and how they are today: “a big city”, “the soup is cold”.
lessons.topic: adjectives after the noun, matching it; {{muy}}; {{es}} or {{está}} with an adjective

goal.t: Mi ciudad es grande y muy bonita.
goal.tr: My city is big and very pretty.

dialog.tr: How are the tacos?
They're really good! And your soup?
It's a little cold.

dialog.t: Es un restaurante muy bueno, pero el mesero está muy ocupado.
dialog.tr: It's a very good restaurant, but the waiter is very busy.

blocks.means: a word that describes a person or a thing: big, red, tired, Mexican.

blocks.p: **After the noun.** In Spanish the adjective usually comes after the noun, the other way round from English: {{una ciudad grande}} “a big city”, {{un carro rojo}} “a red car”, {{el vino blanco}} “the white wine”.

blocks.means: to change so as to match another word. A Spanish adjective agrees with its noun: it takes the noun's gender and number.

blocks.p: **It agrees with its noun**, in gender and in number:

Adjectives ending in **-e** or in a consonant have no feminine form, only a plural: {{un parque grande}}, {{una ciudad grande}}, {{dos ciudades grandes}}; {{un examen difícil}}, {{dos exámenes difíciles}}. {{Muy}} “very” goes before the adjective and never changes: {{muy bonita}}, {{muy grandes}}.
**{{es}} or {{está}}?** With adjectives, {{ser}} says what someone or something is like, {{estar}} how they are now, or how they seem to you right now:

table: {{La sopa de aquí es muy buena.}} The soup here is very good.
{{La sopa está fría.}} The soup is cold.
{{Mi hermana es muy seria.}} My sister is a serious person.
{{Mi hermana está muy seria hoy.}} My sister is very serious today.

blocks.tip: A few common adjectives can go before the noun, and then get shorter: {{bueno}} → {{un buen restaurante}} (a good restaurant), {{malo}} → {{un mal día}} (a bad day), {{grande}} → {{una gran ciudad}} (before the noun it means “great”, not “big”).

mistakes.why: The adjective goes after the noun.
The adjective agrees: {{casas}} is feminine and plural, so {{bonitas}}.
The soup is cold now, not cold by nature: {{está}}.

practice.q: Ana has just run a marathon. “Ana is tired” is…
practice.why: How she is now: {{está}}; and Ana is a woman: {{cansada}}.

practice.tr: Mmm! The tacos are really good.
practice.why: How the food tastes as you eat it: {{están}}.
Being tall is what she's like: {{es}}.

practice.q: At a restaurant: choose your replies.

lines.why: How the food is as you eat it: {{está}}; and {{rica}} for {{la comida}}.

lines.tr: Oh, sorry! I'll bring you another one right away.

practice.q: Your turn: describe your city or town. What's it like? Use {{Mi ciudad es…}} and two adjectives.

answers.t: Mi ciudad es pequeña y muy tranquila.
answers.tr: My city is small and very quiet.

answers.t: Mi ciudad es grande y un poco fea, pero la comida es muy buena.
answers.tr: My city is big and a little ugly, but the food is very good.

lessons.title: Order food and drinks
lessons.summary: Order at a café or a taco stand, and say what you want to do: “I'd like two tacos and a coffee, please.”
lessons.topic: {{quiero}} + a noun; {{quiero}} + an infinitive; {{¿Me da…?}} and {{¿Me trae…?}}

goal.t: Quiero dos tacos y un café, por favor.
goal.tr: I'd like two tacos and a coffee, please.

dialog.tr: Good afternoon. What can I get you?

dialog.t: Para mí, un café con leche, por favor.
dialog.tr: A coffee with milk for me, please.

dialog.t: Yo quiero un jugo de naranja.
dialog.tr: I'd like an orange juice.
Anything to eat?
Yes, we'd like two molletes (bean and cheese rolls).

dialog.t: Muy bien. Ahorita se los traigo.
dialog.tr: Very good. I'll bring them right away.

blocks.p: **Wanting a thing.** {{Quiero}} “I want”, then the thing: {{Quiero un café.}} With {{por favor}} it isn't rude at all: it's the normal way to order. In shops and at stands, Mexicans very often ask {{¿Me da…?}} “Will you give me…?”: {{¿Me da un refresco, por favor?}} And {{Para mí, …}} is “For me, …”: {{Para mí, una limonada.}}

table: he wants, she wants, you want (polite)

blocks.p: Look at the forms: {{quiero}}, {{quieres}}, {{quiere}}, {{quieren}} have **ie**, but {{queremos}} keeps the **e** of {{querer}}. Lesson 19 shows that many verbs do this.

blocks.means: the basic form of a verb, the one in the dictionary: to eat, to go. Spanish infinitives end in -ar, -er or -ir: {{hablar}}, {{comer}}, {{vivir}}.

blocks.p: **Wanting to do something.** After {{quiero}}, the second verb is an infinitive, like English “to …”: {{Quiero comer.}} “I want to eat.” {{Quiero pagar.}} “I want to pay.” There's no word for “to”: the -ar, -er, -ir ending already says it.

ex.t: Quiero una mesa para dos, por favor.
ex.tr: I'd like a table for two, please.
What do you want to drink?
ex.note: {{tomar}} “to take” is also the everyday word for “to drink”

ex.tr: Can I have a kilo of tortillas?
ex.note: word for word “Do you give me…?”: the usual way to ask in a shop

ex.tr: Can I have the check, please?
ex.note: {{¿Me trae…?}} “Will you bring me…?”, at a table

blocks.tip: {{Con}} is “with” and {{sin}} “without”: {{un café sin azúcar}}, {{tacos sin cebolla}}, {{un té con limón}}.

mistakes.why: No word for “to”: the infinitive comes right after {{quiero}}.
“I want” is {{quiero}}, with -o. {{Quiere}} is “he wants”, “she wants”.

practice.q: How do you say “We want to pay”?
practice.why: The infinitive comes right after the verb, and {{queremos}} keeps the e.

practice.q: At a taco stand: choose your replies.

lines.tr: What can I get you, young man?

options: Quiero tres tacos de pastor, por favor.
Quiero a tres tacos de pastor, por favor.
lines.why: {{Quiero}}, then the thing, with nothing in between.

practice.tr: I'd like a table for two, please.

practice.t: ¿Me ___ un kilo de tortillas, por favor?
practice.tr: Can I have a kilo of tortillas, please?
practice.why: {{¿Me da…?}} “Do you give me…?”: the usual way to ask in a shop.

practice.q: Order a coffee without sugar for yourself: “For me, a coffee without sugar, please.”
practice.answer: Para mí, un café sin azúcar, por favor.

practice.q: Your turn: you're at a café in Mexico City. Order something to eat and something to drink.

answers.t: Quiero unos chilaquiles y un café, por favor.
answers.tr: I'd like some chilaquiles and a coffee, please.

answers.t: ¿Me da un pan dulce y un chocolate caliente, por favor?
answers.tr: Can I have a sweet roll and a hot chocolate, please?

lessons.title: Say what you do every day
lessons.summary: Talk about your work, your studies and your day: “I work at a hospital and I study English at night.”
lessons.topic: the present of -ar verbs ({{hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, hablan}}); {{no}} before the verb

goal.t: Trabajo en un hospital y estudio inglés en la noche.
goal.tr: I work at a hospital and I study English at night.

dialog.tr: Do you work or study?

dialog.t: Trabajo. Soy enfermera y trabajo en un hospital.
dialog.tr: I work. I'm a nurse, and I work at a hospital.
And do you speak Spanish at work?

dialog.t: Sí, mucho. Muchos pacientes hablan español.
dialog.tr: Yes, a lot. Lots of patients speak Spanish.

dialog.t: ¡Qué bien! Yo trabajo en una oficina y estudio en la noche.
dialog.tr: Great! I work at an office and study at night.

blocks.p: **Verbs change for each person.** In English, “work” hardly changes: I work, she work**s**. In Spanish the ending changes for every person, and the ending tells you who is doing it. Take the infinitive {{hablar}} “to speak”, drop **-ar**, and add the endings:

blocks.means: to change a verb's ending to show who is doing it: {{hablar}} → {{hablo}} “I speak”, {{hablas}} “you speak”.

blocks.p: Most -ar verbs work exactly like this: {{estudiar}} (to study), {{cocinar}} (to cook), {{escuchar}} (to listen), {{llegar}} (to arrive), {{tomar}} (to take, to drink), {{manejar}} (to drive), {{caminar}} (to walk), {{necesitar}} (to need), {{comprar}} (to buy). One Spanish present covers English “I work”, “I'm working” and “I do work”.

**Who?** Since the ending says who, Spanish usually leaves out {{yo}}, {{tú}} and {{nosotros}}: {{Trabajo en una oficina.}} “He”, “she” and polite “you” share one form, so say the person when it isn't clear: {{Ella trabaja aquí.}} {{¿Usted habla inglés?}}
**Not.** Put {{no}} right before the verb: {{No hablo francés.}} “I don't speak French.” Spanish needs no extra word like “don't”.

ex.tr: We study at the same school.

blocks.tip: In a question the ending does all the work: {{¿Hablas inglés?}} is just {{Hablas inglés}} with a question in your voice. Spanish has no “do” for questions.

mistakes.why: With {{yo}}, the ending is -o: {{trabajo}}.
{{No}} goes right before the verb.

mistakes.wrong: Yo estoy trabajo en un hospital.
mistakes.why: One verb is enough: {{trabajo}} already means “I work”.

practice.tr: My parents work in a store.
Do you speak English? (to a friend)

practice.q: How do you say “We don't need a car”?
practice.why: {{No}} before the verb, and “we” ends in -amos.

practice.q: A new friend asks about your life. Choose your replies.

lines.why: About yourself: -o, {{trabajo}}. And a job without {{un}}: {{Soy ingeniero}}.

options: Trabajo en una empresa en el centro.
Estoy trabajo en una empresa en el centro.

practice.q: Say “I don't speak French, but I speak a little Spanish.”
practice.answer: No hablo francés, pero hablo un poco de español.

practice.q: Your turn: where do you work or study, and what do you do in the evening? Use -ar verbs: {{trabajo, estudio, cocino, escucho…}}

answers.t: Trabajo en una oficina y en la noche cocino con mi esposa.
answers.tr: I work in an office, and in the evening I cook with my wife.

answers.t: Estudio en la universidad y en la noche escucho música.
answers.tr: I study at the university, and in the evening I listen to music.

lessons.title: Say where you live and what you eat
lessons.summary: Talk about your home, your meals and what you read: the verbs ending in -er and -ir.
lessons.topic: the present of -er and -ir verbs ({{como, comes, come…}}, {{vivo, vives, vive…}})

goal.t: Vivo en Guadalajara y como en casa con mi familia.
goal.tr: I live in Guadalajara and I eat at home with my family.

dialog.tr: Where do you live?

dialog.t: Vivo cerca de aquí, en la colonia Roma.
dialog.tr: I live near here, in the Roma neighborhood.
And do you eat here every day?

dialog.t: No, normalmente como en casa. ¿Y tú?
dialog.tr: No, I usually eat at home. And you?

dialog.t: Yo como aquí. Mi esposo y yo vivimos lejos.
dialog.tr: I eat here. My husband and I live far away.

blocks.p: **Two more groups.** Spanish infinitives end in -ar, -er or -ir. You know the -ar endings. Verbs in **-er** and **-ir** use **e** where -ar verbs use **a**, and the two groups are the same except for “we”:

**-er verbs** like {{comer}}: {{beber}} (to drink), {{leer}} (to read), {{aprender}} (to learn), {{vender}} (to sell), {{correr}} (to run), {{creer}} (to believe, to think). **-ir verbs** like {{vivir}}: {{escribir}} (to write), {{abrir}} (to open), {{recibir}} (to receive), {{subir}} (to go up), {{compartir}} (to share).
**The trick:** for “I”, all three groups end in **-o** ({{hablo}}, {{como}}, {{vivo}}). Only “we” shows the infinitive's own vowel: {{hablamos}}, {{comemos}}, {{vivimos}}.

ex.tr: We live in a small apartment.

ex.t: Mi hija aprende inglés en la escuela.
ex.tr: My daughter is learning English at school.

ex.t: La tienda abre a las nueve.

blocks.tip: {{En}} is both “in” and “at”: {{Vivo en Puebla}} (in Puebla), {{Como en casa}} (at home), {{Trabajo en un banco}} (at a bank).

mistakes.why: {{vivir}} is an -ir verb, so “we” is {{vivimos}}.
{{No}} goes right before the verb.
“I” always ends in -o: {{vivo}}.

practice.t: Los domingos ___ tacos en casa de mi abuela.
practice.tr: On Sundays we eat tacos at my grandmother's house.

lessons.title: Ask questions
lessons.summary: Ask for information: what, who, where, when, how, how much and why.
lessons.topic: yes/no questions; {{qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cómo, cuánto, por qué, cuál}}

goal.tr: What are you studying, and why?

dialog.tr: What are you studying?
I'm studying medicine.
Why medicine?
Because my mom is a doctor.
And when do you finish?
In two years. And you? What are you studying?

blocks.p: **Yes or no.** The simplest question is an ordinary sentence with your voice going up at the end: {{Hablas inglés.}} “You speak English.” → {{¿Hablas inglés?}} “Do you speak English?” Spanish needs no “do”. In writing, a question opens with ¿ and closes with ?.
**Question words** come first, and they always carry an accent mark:
**Why and because.** {{¿Por qué?}}, two words with an accent, asks “why?”; {{porque}}, one word with no accent, answers “because”: {{¿Por qué estudias español? — Porque vivo en México.}}
**After the question word** comes the verb, and then the person, if you name one: {{¿Dónde trabaja tu hermano?}} “Where does your brother work?”, word for word “where works your brother?”.

**Little words go first.** A word like {{de}} “from” or {{con}} “with” goes before the question word, never at the end as in English: {{¿De dónde eres?}} “Where are you from?” {{¿Con quién vives?}} “Who do you live with?”

ex.tr: How do you say “thank you” in Spanish?
What do you eat for breakfast?

ex.note: “What is your…?” asking for a name, a number or an address: {{cuál}}

blocks.tip: When you don't catch what someone said, Mexicans say {{¿Mande?}} “Pardon?”: polite, and very Mexican. {{¿Cómo?}} also works; {{¿Qué?}} on its own can sound rude.

mistakes.why: The little word {{de}} goes before the question word, never at the end.

mistakes.wrong: ¿Por qué estudias español? — Por qué vivo en México.
mistakes.right: ¿Por qué estudias español? — Porque vivo en México.
mistakes.tr: Why are you studying Spanish? — Because I live in Mexico.
mistakes.why: The answer “because” is one word with no accent: {{porque}}.
Asking for a piece of information (a name, a number), Spanish says {{¿Cuál es…?}}; {{¿Qué es…?}} asks for a definition. (Most people simply ask {{¿Cómo te llamas?}})

practice.tr: Where do you live? — In Monterrey.

practice.q: Your friend asks {{¿Por qué estudias español?}} Which answer is right?
practice.why: “Because” is one word with no accent: {{porque}}.

lessons.title: Talk about your family and your age
lessons.summary: Say who's in your family, how old people are, and whose things are whose: {{tengo}}, {{mi}}, {{tu}}, {{su}}.
lessons.topic: {{tener}} ({{tengo, tienes, tiene…}}); {{mi, tu, su, nuestro}}; {{tener … años}} for age

goal.t: Tengo un hermano y una hermana. Mi hermana tiene veinte años.
goal.tr: I have a brother and a sister. My sister is twenty.

dialog.tr: Who's he?

dialog.t: Es mi hermano Leo. Tiene treinta años.
dialog.tr: That's my brother Leo. He's thirty.
And does he have kids?

dialog.t: Sí, tiene dos hijas. Son mis sobrinas.
dialog.tr: Yes, he has two daughters. They're my nieces.
How cute! What about you? Do you have kids?
No, but I have a dog.

blocks.p: **{{tener}} “to have”** is one of the most used verbs in Spanish, and it's irregular: learn it by heart.

table: he has, she has, you have (polite)

blocks.p: **Age is something you have.** Spanish says how many years you **have**: {{Tengo treinta años.}} “I'm thirty”, word for word “I have thirty years”. Ask with {{¿Cuántos años tienes?}} “How old are you?”

blocks.means: a word that says whose something is: my, your, his, our.

blocks.p: **my, your, his…** go before the noun. They match the number of the things owned (one or more), not the owner; {{nuestro}} “our” also matches their gender:

{{su}} can be his, her, their or polite “your”: the situation makes it clear. When it doesn't, use {{de}} and the person: {{la casa de Ana}} “Ana's house”. Spanish has no 's: it says “the house of Ana”.

**Family words**: {{papá}}, {{mamá}}, {{papás}} (parents), {{hermano}} / {{hermana}}, {{hijo}} / {{hija}}, {{esposo}} / {{esposa}}, {{abuelo}} / {{abuela}}, {{tío}} / {{tía}}, {{primo}} / {{prima}} (cousin), {{sobrino}} / {{sobrina}} (nephew, niece). A masculine plural covers a mixed group: {{mis hermanos}} can be brothers and sisters, {{mis hijos}} sons and daughters.

ex.t: Ella es la esposa de mi hermano.

blocks.tip: Numbers for ages: {{veinte}} (20), {{treinta}} (30), {{cuarenta}} (40), {{cincuenta}} (50), {{sesenta}} (60), {{setenta}} (70), {{ochenta}} (80). In between, with {{y}}: {{treinta y cinco}} (35). From 16 to 29 they are one word: {{dieciocho}} (18), {{veinticinco}} (25).

mistakes.why: In Spanish you have your age: {{tener}}.
One brother: {{mi}}. {{mis}} is for more than one.
Spanish has no 's: “the car of Juan”, {{el carro de Juan}}.

practice.why: To a friend, and more than one: {{tus}}.
Spanish has no 's: {{la casa de Ana}}, “the house of Ana”.

lessons.title: Say what you like
lessons.summary: Say what you like and don't like, and ask others: “I really like tacos, but I don't like very spicy food.”
lessons.topic: {{me gusta}} and {{me gustan}}; {{te, le, nos, les}}; {{a mí también}}, {{a mí tampoco}}

goal.t: Me gustan mucho los tacos, pero no me gusta la comida muy picante.
goal.tr: I really like tacos, but I don't like very spicy food.

dialog.tr: Do you like Mexican music?

dialog.t: Sí, me gusta mucho. Me gustan los mariachis.
dialog.tr: Yes, I like it a lot. I like mariachi bands.
And do you like to dance?
Not really. How about you?
I do, a lot!

blocks.means: who or what does the verb: in “Ana works”, it's Ana. In Spanish the verb's ending matches its subject.

blocks.p: **Back to front.** Spanish doesn't say “I like coffee”. It says {{Me gusta el café}}: “coffee pleases me”. The thing you like is the subject, the verb {{gusta}} goes with it, and {{me}} “to me” says who likes it.
**One thing or more?** The verb matches the thing you like: {{gusta}} for one thing, or for doing something; {{gustan}} for more than one thing:
**Who likes it?** Change the little word in front:

table: he likes, she likes, you like (polite)

blocks.p: Spanish keeps “the” even for things in general: {{Me gusta el café}}, {{Me gustan los perros}} “I like dogs”.

**Me too, me neither.** Answer with {{a}} and the person: {{A mí también.}} “Me too.” {{A mí tampoco.}} “Me neither” (after a “not”). {{A mí sí.}} / {{A mí no.}} when you feel differently. {{¿Y a ti?}} turns it back: “And you?”. The same {{a}} names who: {{A mi papá le gusta el fútbol.}} “My dad likes soccer.”

ex.t: No me gustan las películas de terror.
A mis hijos les gusta mucho nadar.
Nos gusta caminar en el parque.
ex.tr: We like to walk in the park.

blocks.tip: {{Mucho}} goes after {{gusta}}: {{Me gusta mucho.}} “I like it a lot.” And {{¿Te gusta?}} with nothing after it means “Do you like it?”: no word for “it” is needed.

mistakes.why: {{gustar}} works back to front: “coffee pleases me”, {{me gusta}}.
More than one thing: {{gustan}}.
Spanish keeps the article when you talk about something in general.

practice.q: Your friend says {{No me gusta el café.}} You don't like it either. You say…

lessons.title: Shop: this one, that one, how much?
lessons.summary: Point to what you want in a shop or at a market, and ask the price: “How much is this T-shirt?”
lessons.topic: {{este, ese}} (and {{aquel}}); {{esto, eso}}; {{¿Cuánto cuesta?}} and {{¿Cuánto cuestan?}}; numbers to a thousand

goal.tr: How much is this T-shirt? — Two hundred pesos.

dialog.tr: Good afternoon. How much is this hat?
That one is three hundred pesos.
And those?
Those are two hundred fifty.
Hmm… Would you let me have it for two hundred?
Okay then. Two hundred.

blocks.means: a word that points: this, that, these, those.

blocks.p: **This and that.** {{este}} is “this” (near me), {{ese}} is “that” (near you, or a little way off). Like adjectives, they match the noun:

They also stand alone for “this one”, “that one”: {{Quiero ese.}} “I want that one.” For something you can't name, or an idea, use {{esto}} and {{eso}}, which never change: {{¿Qué es esto?}} {{Eso es.}} “That's it.” For something far from both of you there's {{aquel}} “that … over there” ({{aquella casa}}), but in everyday Mexican Spanish {{ese}} usually does the job.
**How much?** The verb {{costar}} “to cost” matches the thing: {{¿Cuánto cuesta?}} for one, {{¿Cuánto cuestan?}} for more than one. The answer: {{Cuesta cien pesos.}} {{Cuestan cincuenta.}}

Build bigger numbers piece by piece, with {{y}} only between the tens and the ones: {{treinta y cinco}} (35), {{ciento treinta y cinco}} (135), {{mil doscientos}} (1,200). {{cien}} is exactly 100; above it, {{ciento}}.

ex.tr: I want that one, the red one.

ex.t: ¿Me da un kilo de esas naranjas?
ex.tr: Can I have a kilo of those oranges?

blocks.tip: At markets, prices are often said without {{pesos}}: {{Son ochenta.}} “That's eighty.” {{¿Me hace un descuento?}} “Can you give me a discount?” is worth knowing too.

mistakes.why: More than one thing: {{cuestan}}.
{{playera}} is feminine: {{esta}}.

mistakes.tr: It costs a hundred fifty pesos.
mistakes.why: Above 100 it's {{ciento}}, and {{y}} goes only between the tens and the ones.

practice.why: The hundreds are one word, and {{y}} goes only between tens and ones.
